bib.title: Explaining Models: An Empirical Study of How Explanations Impact Fairness Judgment

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Explaining Models: An Empirical Study of How Explanations Impact Fairness Judgment", Jonathan Dodge, Q. Vera Liao, Yunfeng Zhang, Rachel K. E. Bellamy, Casey Dugan. IUI 2019 (arXiv:1901.07694v1).

COVERAGE: 69,210 of 69,210 chars, all 10 pages. References read too. Nothing skipped. Quotes were checked by script against the page text. Line breaks are collapsed and end-of-line hyphens rejoined; otherwise they are verbatim.

CLAIMS

- claim: Local explanations widened the rated gap between disparately impacted and non-impacted cases more than global ones, but the omnibus test was only marginal and one pairwise contrast was significant.
  number: p = 0.07 (omnibus); p = 0.02 (sensitivity vs influence); p = 0.07 (sensitivity vs demographic); p = 0.07 (case vs influence)
  setup: mixed-effects regression, participant as random effect, gender and race as controls; outcome is a 1-7 fairness rating. The authors call 0.05 <= p < 0.10 "marginally significant".
  quote: "two-way interaction between explanation style and disparate impact, F(3, 152) = 2.35, p = 0.07"; "influence-based explanation is significantly different, F(1, 156) = 5.14, p = 0.02"; "F(1, 156) = 3.29, p = 0.07"; "F(1, 156) = 3.36, p = 0.07"
  where: p6

- claim: The expected three-way interaction (style x data processing x disparate impact) failed in the base model and became significant only after individual differences were added.
  number: p = 0.66 before; p = 0.03 after
  setup: same design; the second model adds race position and ML position.
  quote: "The three-way interaction we expected is not significant, F(3, 152) = 0.54, p = 0.66"; "to be significant, F(3, 144) = 2.96, p = 0.03"
  where: p6, p7

- claim: Sensitivity explanations lowered perceived fairness on race-flipped cases only for people who already considered using race unfair.
  number: four-way p = 0.05; 33.1% considered race fair-to-neutral
  setup: race position split at race_pos < 4 in Figure 3. The fair-to-neutral group did not rate raw-data predictions as less fair than processed-data ones.
  quote: "factors, F(3, 144) = 2.59, p = 0.05"; "it is only when an individual considers using race to be unfair"; "fair-to-neutral (33.1% of all participants)"
  where: p7

- claim: Prior positions had significant main effects on perceived fairness; need for cognition made no difference and was dropped.
  number: ML position p < 0.001; race position p = 0.01; ML position x style p = 0.07
  setup: no effect sizes or coefficients are reported, only F and p. Need for cognition used a shortened scale (see LIMITS).
  quote: "F(1, 137) = 17.31, p < 0.001"; "F(1, 137) = 6.43, p = 0.01"; "F(3, 137) = 2.43, p = 0.07"; "possibly more so than differences in cognitive styles"
  where: p7

- claim: Participants rated cases with disparate impact as less fair, and predictions from the debiased model as fairer.
  number: disparate impact p < 0.001; data processing p = 0.03
  setup: base model. With individual differences added: F(1, 144) = 28.86, p < 0.001 and F(1, 137) = 4.68, p = 0.03.
  quote: "F(1, 152) = 103.25, p < 0.001"; "F(1, 152) = 4.65, p = 0.03"
  where: p6, p7

- claim: Explanation style had at most a marginal main effect, visible only after controlling for individual factors; case-based was rated marginally less fair than both global styles.
  number: p = 0.10 (main); p = 0.06 and p = 0.08 (pairwise)
  setup: the authors nonetheless treat this as "evidence that case-based explanation is seen as generally less fair".
  quote: "style, F(3, 137) = 2.11, p = 0.10"; "F(1, 153) = 3.51, p = 0.06"; "F(1, 148) = 3.20, p = 0.08"
  where: p7

- claim: Participants with higher trust in ML gained more confidence from global explanations.
  number: p = 0.01; p = 0.05; marginal p = 0.10
  setup: ML position x style pairwise comparisons. See PROBLEMS: two of these state the same reference level.
  quote: "F(1, 148) = 6.25, p = 0.01"; "F(1, 148) = 3.73, p = 0.05"; "F(1, 148) = 2.77, p = 0.10"
  where: p7

- claim: Case-based explanations are often unsound on this data, contradicting or barely supporting the prediction.
  number: 16% contradict; 24% insufficient
  setup: test data; contradiction is under 50% of identical individuals sharing the label, insufficient is 45-55% matches. The ranges overlap as printed.
  quote: "16% of the test data exhibited the failure mode"; "with 24% of the test data"
  where: p9, footnote 6

- claim: The model is a scikit-learn logistic regression on a COMPAS subset, with accuracy near COMPAS itself.
  number: 67.1% raw, 67.6% processed; 4222 train, 1056 test
  setup: two racial groups only; features are race, age, charge degree, prior convictions, juvenile convictions.
  quote: "The accuracy of the model is 67.1% on raw data and 67.6% on processed data"; "training set (4222 samples) and testing set (1056)"
  where: p4

- claim: Calmon et al. preprocessing shrank the race coefficient to near zero.
  number: 0.177 to -0.036
  setup: retrained logistic regression.
  quote: "reduced from 0.177 to -0.036"
  where: p4

- claim: Disparately impacted cases were rare, near the decision boundary, and deliberately oversampled.
  number: 23 cases (8 unique); 16 unique sampled of 992 non-impacted; confidence average 52%, max 54%
  setup: disparate impact means flipping race changes the prediction. Each participant saw 2 impacted and 4 non-impacted trials. The processed classifier had average and max confidence both at 50%.
  quote: "We found 23 cases in the raw dataset"; "we sampled all 8 unique cases"; "From the non-impacted group of 992 instances, we sampled 16 unique cases"; "an average of 52% and a max of 54%"
  where: p4

- claim: The sample was 160 US Mechanical Turk workers across 8 between-subject conditions, each judging 6 cases.
  number: 160; 8 conditions; 6 trials; 18 min; 62.5% male
  setup: September 2018; over 1000 tasks and at least 98% approval; 78.8% Caucasian; paid $3. Participant race and gender had no significant effect.
  quote: "we recruited 160 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers"; "Each participant completed 6 fairness judgment trials"; "On average the study took 18 min"; "62.5% are male"
  where: p5

- claim: Close to a third of participants considered race neutral or fair to use, despite its protected status.
  number: "close to one third" (33.1% on p7)
  setup: semantic differential, 5 adjective pairs on a 7-point scale, Cronbach alpha 0.95 (ML) and 0.98 (race).
  quote: "close to one third of participants considered it neutral or fair to use"; "The Cronbach Alpha for the scale on general ML position is 0.95"
  where: p9, p6

- claim: The authors conclude that no explanation suits all cases, and propose hybrid global-plus-local explanations and personalisation.
  number: none
  setup: the hybrid workflow was proposed in discussion, not tested.
  quote: "no one-size-fits-all solution"
  where: p9

Qualitative, no numbers (p8-9, authors' open coding):
- Influence explanations add confidence but expose more to critique.
- Demographic explanations draw attention to data bias.
- Sensitivity explanations are concise, and were perceived most negatively on race-flip cases.
- Case-based explanations were judged least fair.
- The authors report a general preference for process-oriented over data-oriented explanations.

LIMITS
- Conceded (p9): crowdworkers, not judges; many explanation styles and elements not studied; confidence not shown to participants because it could not be controlled.
- The authors state the goal is not to study actual COMPAS users; the use case is a "probe" (p3).
- The outcome is self-rated perceived fairness on one item. There is no decision task, no measure of accuracy in detecting unfairness, and no measure of downstream behaviour.
- My observations, not conceded:
  - No effect sizes are reported.
  - Pairwise tests show no stated multiple-comparison correction.
  - Many key results are marginal by the authors' own label.
  - The individual-difference model was reached by iteratively reducing terms, and it is what rescued the three-way interaction.
  - Impacted cases all sit near 50% confidence, so impact and boundary position cannot be separated. The authors do describe them as near the boundary.
  - Roughly 20 people per cell (160 / 8, derived).
- Need for cognition used 4 items of the standard scale: "using only 4 of the items" (p6). Its null is weak evidence.
- Dated: pre-LLM, and only template explanations of a five-feature logistic regression. Results may not transfer to other models or domains; the paper tests one domain.

BUILDS ON
- Binns et al. 2018 [5]: the four explanation types, and the study it directly extends.
- Calmon et al. 2017 [9]: the preprocessor.
- Grgic-Hlaca et al. 2018 [14]: the descriptive fairness view and same use case.
- Wick and Thompson 1992 [37], Swartout 1985 [33]: global-local and how-versus-why.
- Kulesza et al. 2013 [20]: soundness and completeness.
- Calders and Žliobaitė 2013 [8]: the disparate impact definition.
- Cacioppo et al. 1984 [7]: need for cognition.
- Liao and Fu 2014 [24]: the attitude scale.
- Cramer and Howitt 2004 [12]: the "marginally significant" convention.

CODE: none in the paper.

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p5: examples of the four explanation styles from the raw-data classifier. Best candidate: it shows the styles at a glance, including the "if it had been Caucasian" sensitivity wording.
- Fig 2, p6: mean fairness ratings per style, data treatment and impact group, with 95% CIs. Shows the local-versus-global gap directly.
- Fig 3, p6: Fig 2 split by prior position on race. Shows the sensitivity effect appearing only in the "unfair" group.
- Fig 4, p7: mean ratings by trust in ML. Shows the high-trust boost from global styles.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions. Extraction is clean except that figure plots extract as stray markers and axis numbers, and some legend symbols are lost from captions. I read figure captions, not plot images.
- Internal inconsistencies in the source:
  - n: abstract says "more than 160"; methodology says exactly 160.
  - p7 twice says "using case-based explanation as the reference" with different F values (6.25 and 3.73). One reference level is probably a typo; I cannot tell which.
  - 23 impacted + 992 non-impacted = 1015, but the test set is 1056. Unexplained.
  - p7 calls a p = 0.05 term significant and p = 0.10 terms marginal, although footnote 4 defines marginal as p < 0.10. Probably rounding.
  - Figure 1's panel lists juvenile priors as "No priors, 1-3, >3"; p4 text says True/False.
  - The ACM reference on p1 prints "Marina del Ray".

COMPARISON WITH THE NOTE
/Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/data-science/01-classical-ml/notes/08-model-interpretability.md line 282:
"More than 160 Mechanical Turk workers, four explanation styles | Global and local styles reveal different fairness problems, and a person's prior position strongly shapes the reaction"

Correct: authors, arXiv id, IUI 2019, four styles, and the general direction of both findings.

Mismatches and under-qualified claims, most important first:

1. "Global and local styles reveal different fairness problems" overstates the result. The data support one half: local beats global on case-specific discrepancies, and that rests on an omnibus p = 0.07 with a single significant pairwise contrast. No result shows global styles better at revealing model-wide unfairness.
   - RQ1b has no positive finding. The data-processing effect is reported as a main effect, not moderated by global style.
   - The reported global finding is different: they "seem to render more confidence in understanding the model and generally enhance the fairness perception" (p9). That is raised perceived fairness, arguably the opposite of revealing a problem, and for the high-trust subgroup in the summary on p7.
   - The abstract itself hedges: "may be more effectively exposed through different styles of explanation".

2. "strongly shapes" has no support as a strength claim. No effect sizes are given. The paper's wording is "significant impact" (p7). The race-position four-way term is p = 0.05, and ML position x style is p = 0.07. The ML position main effect (p < 0.001) is on fairness ratings overall, not on the reaction to a style. Also unstated: the specific form, that sensitivity explanations lowered fairness ratings only for people who already saw race as unfair.

3. Missing setup. The row omits:
   - the domain: COMPAS recidivism, race as the protected feature;
   - the model: a logistic regression on five features, about 67% accurate, with explanations programmatically generated;
   - the outcome: a single 1-7 perceived-fairness rating over 6 trials;
   - the sample limit: US crowdworkers, not judges;
   - the oversampling of near-boundary disparate cases.
   The neighbouring Wang and Yin row names its tasks, so the omission of domain stands out.

4. The outcome is unnamed under the section "Does explaining help anyone?". "Reveal" and "reaction" read as if detection or help was measured. The study measured perceived fairness, not decision quality or whether fairness was correctly judged. The closing advice and the pitfall "Evaluate decisions made with the explanation" sit beside this row, but this study did not evaluate decisions.

5. "More than 160" follows the abstract; the methods section says 160 exactly ("we recruited 160"). The F-test degrees of freedom are consistent with 160. Recommend "160".

6. Related row, /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/data-science/01-classical-ml/references.md line 53: "Explanation style changes fairness judgements". The main effect of style is only marginal (p = 0.10) and appears only after controlling for individual factors; the effect is mainly an interaction with case type and prior position. Under-qualified in the same way. The linked PDF exists at data-science/sources/dodge-2019-explaining-models.pdf, with the same file size as the copy I read.

Bookkeeping: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/scripts/papers/ledger.jsonl line 643 has status "queued", with reason "has no matching note", yet the note cites this paper.

Suggested facts for a corrected row, for the caller to decide on:
- Setup: 160 US MTurk workers rating 1-7 perceived fairness of a logistic regression on COMPAS, four template explanation styles.
- Finding: local styles exposed case-specific disparities more than global ones (marginal overall, p = 0.07; sensitivity vs influence p = 0.02); sensitivity explanations lowered ratings only for people who already saw race as unfair; global styles raised perceived fairness among those who trusted ML.
